title: Show HN: Cerulion – Harness for Robotics, Gemini 3.8 Flash Matches GPT-6 Astra
author: lakshays
snippet: Hey HN! I'm Lakshay, and at Cerulion we cooked up a harness for physical AI. Built on top of our deterministic runtime, we now have MCP tools that let any LLM see and move a robot. It closes the loop with measurements so a model doesn't try to guess its way through the task…
excerpt: Hey HN! I'm Lakshay, and at Cerulion we cooked up a harness for physical AI. Built on top of our deterministic runtime, we now have MCP tools that let any LLM see and move a robot. It closes the loop with measurements so a model doesn't try to guess its way through the task, and imbues common sense and robotics best practices into the workflow. We ran the numbers on LIBERO-PRO and quite frankly are a bit shocked. Gemini 3.8 Flash with Cerulion solved 73 of 100 LIBERO-PRO tasks. GPT-6 Astra on a bare 3-tool baseline (arXiv:2610.30051) solved 71, at about 12x the cost and 3x the wall time per run. Flash on that same baseline solved 25. Guys. Gemini 3.8 Flash matched GPT-6 Astra for robotics. Model intelligence is not the bottleneck. A harness is all you need ;) Star us and follow along. Try the quickstart, lmk what you guys wanna see next. I'll post again soon! (teaser: my Nespresso machine is getting a lot of attention from my robot arm)

title: Show HN: Mole – research agent that traces claims to their sources
author: lajosd
snippet: I originally started building Mole as an open-source tool a couple of months ago, because I was annoyed with my LLMs returning super confident answers to my questions about facts, numbers, statistics, etc. They basically recited big claims from news articles, about which I'm…
excerpt: I originally started building Mole as an open-source tool a couple of months ago, because I was annoyed with my LLMs returning super confident answers to my questions about facts, numbers, statistics, etc. They basically recited big claims from news articles, about which I'm naturally skeptical. And of course, once I manually traced a few of these to their sources, they turned out to be subpar, or downright incorrect. So I came up with Mole, a tool that searches and reads sources, extracts claims, checks each against a verbatim quote from the page, and flags disagreements between the sources. The OS version just got v0.3.0 released today, the biggest feature of this release is that it now tries to go all the way through the very origin of a statistic to see where it originally came from. Besides this, the hosted version runs the OS core, but it researches any question for you without installing anything, and creates a clean, downloadable research report that you can carry with you into a business meeting, an academic presentation, or any such place. Hope you find it useful and leave me some feedback!

title: Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton
snippet: Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton TL;DR Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a…
excerpt: Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton TL;DR Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a controller in Isaac Lab to adjust gamepad velocity commands around obstacles. This tutorial covers simulation training, evaluation, export, and real-robot deployment. Introduction A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path. In this workflow, we reuse the walking policy from our first Microduck tutorial and keep its weights fixed. This follow-up trains a separate avoidance controller using time-of-flight (ToF) sensing. You choose a direction with a gamepad; the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy. NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment. Newton simulates physics and the sensor’s depth measurements. We will cover the control architecture, train on varied obstacle layouts, evaluate the resulting policies, and prepare the interface for hardware testing. 1. Set Microduck obstacle avoidance in Isaac Lab For simulation and training, prepare: - A Linux system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver. See the Isaac Lab installation guide for platform requirements. - Git with Git LFS, and the uv package manager. For physical-robot testing, prepare: - A configured Microduck. Load the same backlash walking-policy export used by the navigation task. - A supported ToF sensor with its configuration recorded. - A paired gamepad and a level test area with obstacles. Quick install Install uv if it is not already installed. Then clone the exp/microduck branch of the Isaac Lab repository and install its dependencies: git lfs install git clone --branch exp/microduck cd IsaacLab uv…

title: Four C/C++ libraries ported to pure managed .NET on a $20 plan
author: sensboston
snippet: I'm between jobs right now, and I'm bad at sitting idle. I could have built yet another portfolio site with a chatbot and a smiling robot avatar, but I wanted to spend the time on something people might actually use. There was a second reason. My feed is full of stories about…
excerpt: I'm between jobs right now, and I'm bad at sitting idle. I could have built yet another portfolio site with a chatbot and a smiling robot avatar, but I wanted to spend the time on something people might actually use. There was a second reason. My feed is full of stories about LLM agents that burn thousands of dollars in tokens overnight. I suspected that most of them say more about the process than about the tools, and I wanted to check that on real work. So over about three weeks, with Claude Code on a $20/month Pro plan as the main tool (plus $100 of promotional credits that were expiring anyway, and some free-tier model sessions for the routine parts), I ported four native libraries to fully managed C#, with no P/Invoke and no native binaries: - Leptonica.Managed - Leptonica 1.87.0, image processing and the base of Tesseract OCR; about 2,700 functions. - Stb.Managed - seven of Sean Barrett's stb libraries (image load/save, resize, TrueType, rect_pack, DXT, Perlin). - MetadataSharp - EXIF/MakerNotes, IPTC, XMP and ICC read/write. Not a port: written from the specs, with Exiv2 as the reference. - MdfLibrary.Managed - mdflib, the ASAM MDF format of automotive data loggers, with the same API as its Windows-only C++/CLI wrapper, plus a cross-platform viewer with live CAN capture. All four are on NuGet under MIT. I wouldn't call this vibe coding. The model wrote most of the code, but the work went the way any port of this size should go, with or without an LLM. First we discussed the architecture: what maps to what in C#, what stays bit-exact and what may be optimized, what is ported and what is left out. Then came a written plan in stages, each with a measurable exit condition. Before the first line of the port, the native library was built and became the oracle; the tests compare against it, not against the model's opinion of what the output should be. title: Show HN: Yolt – Your Personal TV
author: joonfjp
snippet: Clipping tools are ubiquitous these days. Videos can be bulky, and hosted options are expensive. Yolt never stores a video, full or clipped. A clip is just a start and end time on the original YouTube video, played through YouTube’s embedded player. An LLM ranks the best…
excerpt: Clipping tools are ubiquitous these days. Videos can be bulky, and hosted options are expensive. Yolt never stores a video, full or clipped. A clip is just a start and end time on the original YouTube video, played through YouTube’s embedded player. An LLM ranks the best moments, and new episodes are clipped automatically. The TV tab plays all your clips back to back, with a QR code to open the full episode on your phone at that timestamp. Semantic search requires an embeddings endpoint, which you set with YOLT_EMBED_URL. Without one, exact-word search still works. Self-hosted, runs with make, works with any OpenAI-compatible LLM. Feedback is welcome!
